research_text:
# Research brief: java.security.KeyPairGenerator and the "invalid key size for algorithm RSA" finding

## Source limits
- **I could not retrieve the rule file.** The raw URL for `KeyPairGenerator.crysl` was not returned by my search tool, and I could not fetch pages directly. I found no text of that file, so I cannot quote its matching clause verbatim. Question 4 is therefore largely unanswered from the primary source (see that section).
- Everything about the rule's contents in the supplied input is secondary. I did not verify it against the file.
- I did not determine the rule-pack commit or CryptoAnalysis version.
- The search results were excerpts, not full pages.

## Q1. What KeyPairGenerator governs, and what the finding refers to
- **What the class does.** `java.security.KeyPairGenerator` generates public/private key pairs for a named algorithm. The Javadoc says the keysize is interpreted differently per algorithm, and that for DSA it is the modulus length. For RSA the key size is the modulus size. Sources:
  - https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html
  - https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html
  - https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder (RSA modulus size, in the Android setting)
- **Documented events and values.** `initialize(int keysize)` and `initialize(int keysize, SecureRandom)` take the key size. `initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec[, SecureRandom])` takes a parameter set instead.
- **Runtime exceptions.** Per the Javadoc, `initialize(int)` throws `InvalidParameterException` "if the keysize is not supported by this KeyPairGenerator object." The parameter-spec overloads declare `InvalidAlgorithmParameterException`. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html
- **"Invalid key size" is not a Javadoc term.** It is a detector message from the CrySL rule. The only documented API-level counterpart I found is the `InvalidParameterException` above, which is provider-dependent.
- **Naming overlap.** The spec name `KeyPairGeneratorSpec` matches `android.security.KeyPairGeneratorSpec`, a different class. It is an `AlgorithmParameterSpec` used with a `KeyPairGenerator` from the AndroidKeyStore provider. It is deprecated since API level 23, and `KeyGenParameterSpec` replaces it. See https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyPairGeneratorSpec. The governed type in the input is `java.security.KeyPairGenerator`, and I did not find a stated link between the two.

## Q2. Documented correct usage and remediation
- **Default initialization.** The Javadoc says that if the client does not call `initialize`, "each provider must supply (and document) a default initialization." The Sun provider's DSA default is cited as an example. See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html. Skipping `initialize` is therefore documented as allowed, and the default is provider-specific.
- **Algorithm names.** They come from the Standard Algorithm Names specification, e.g. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- **Required sizes.** The JDK 26 Javadoc says every implementation must support these sizes:
  - RSA: 1024, 2048, 3072, 4096
  - DiffieHellman: 1024, 2048, 3072, 4096
  - DSA: 1024, 2048
  - RSASSA-PSS: 2048, 3072, 4096
  - EC: curves secp256r1 and secp384r1

  JDK 8 listed only RSA (1024, 2048), DSA (1024) and DiffieHellman (1024). Sources:
  - https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html
  - https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html
- **Provider limits.** The JDK 21 provider documentation says SunRsaSign RSA keys must be between 512 and 16384 bits. The default is 3072, and above 3072 the public exponent length is limited to 64 bits. SunMSCAPI RSA ranges from 512 to 16384 depending on the underlying Windows provider, with a default of 2048. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/oracle-providers.html
- **Default RSA size change.** JDK-8282995 raised the SunRsaSign, SunJCE, SunEC and SunPKCS11 defaults: RSA and DH from 2048 to 3072, and EC from 256 to 384. See https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/jdk-8282995. This is an issue tracker page, not a specification. I did not confirm the JDK release in which it landed.
- **Remediation.** I found no official statement of remediation for an "invalid key size" finding. Javadoc only documents the exceptions, and the provider pages document supported sizes. Choosing a size or a fix is outside this brief.
- **Android.** `KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder.setKeySize` says the default key size is algorithm-specific. If no size is set, it is looked up from the algorithm-specific parameters. See https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder

## Q3. Compatibility
- **Persisted and wire formats.** I found no official statement in the `KeyPairGenerator` sources about key size affecting persisted or wire formats. The JCA guide's Diffie-Hellman samples show keys exchanged as encoded key material, and a peer's DH parameters being reused. See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.htm. I found no compatibility rule beyond that. Whether a size change affects stored keys, certificates, or peers is unresolved.
- **Platform support.** The required-size lists above differ by JDK version, and provider defaults changed between releases. The Javadoc text on Sun DSA precomputed parameters also varies by version. It says 512/768/1024 on JDK 7 and 8, and adds 2048 in the Android text. The JDK 9 JCA guide lists 512, 768, 1024, 2048 and 3072.
- **Android.** Android's `KeyPairGenerator` documentation lists RSA as supported from API level 1. See https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyPairGenerator. `KeyPairGeneratorSpec` was added in API 18 and deprecated in API 23, with `KeyGenParameterSpec` as the documented replacement. The `KeyPairGeneratorSpec` page says `getKeySize()` returns the key size specified by the spec. See https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyPairGeneratorSpec. Android Keystore key material is non-exportable, per https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore. I found no documented procedure for migrating existing keys to a different size.

## Q4. What the CrySL rule applies
- **Not verified from the file.** I could not read `KeyPairGenerator.crysl`, so I cannot report its method names, receiver types, parameter-list constraints or conditions, and I cannot quote a clause. Search results for the file returned only the sibling `KeyPair.crysl` (https://github.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/blob/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl) and the repository landing pages.
- **What CrySL documents in general.** The Eclipse CogniCrypt documentation (https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/) says:
  - The `SPEC` clause names the fully qualified class the rule applies to.
  - The `EVENTS` block lists the method calls on that class's objects.
  - The `ORDER` block is a regular expression over event labels.
  - Argument values bound to rule variables can be constrained in `CONSTRAINTS`.

  That documentation describes the language, not this rule's clauses.
- **Can it match a same-named method on another type?** I cannot state this from the rule source. The generic documentation implies matching is tied to the class in `SPEC`, but that is an inference about CrySL, not a finding about this file.
- **Inconsistency in the supplied input.**
  - The reported message concerns RSA. The `detector_semantics` claim says the finding is "consistent with the reported DSA clause."
  - The RSA predicate quoted in the input is `keysize in {4096, 3072}`.
  - Any claim about which clause fired needs the actual rule file and an analysis trace.
- **Other unresolved items.**
  - Whether the detector treats a `KeyPairGeneratorSpec` argument to `initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec)` as relevant to key-size constraints.
  - Whether the algorithm and size values were resolved or imprecisely extracted.
